extracted.intended_audience: USPTO rulemakers and patent practitioners (corporate IP leaders, patent attorneys, interested stakeholders)
extracted.subtask_description: A formal corporate comment submitted to the USPTO arguing against a proposed rulemaking that would change terminal disclaimer practice and link continuation/child patents to parent patents. The document evaluates legal, practical, and policy implications of the proposed change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal Disclaimer Practice purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuation/Terminal Disclaimer practice primarily serves to refine claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuation patents with further refinements are an essential part of the patent system and afford the applicant the ability to refine the claim language by, for example, broadening claims, narrowing claims, focusing on different aspects of the invention, accommodating real world infringement conditions or changes to patent law. The current terminal disclaimer practice prohibits abuse of term extension by limiting the term of “child” patents to the term of the parent along with ownership restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow iterative claim refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must be able to iterate claim language across continuations to obtain 'good' patents; claiming is complex and small details can render claims unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be a mechanism for applicants to claim their justifiably earned rights in an optimal fashion while allowing for human error, better understanding of the prior art presented during examination, adaptation to rapid changes in the usage environment and changes in the law. The current system of claim refinements over several continuations may yield only a single enforceable patent after several iterations; without iterations an applicant could only gain rights by perfecting the initial prosecution or engaging in complex (and expensive) maneuvers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not unidirectionally link child to parent beyond term/ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer should not link a child application's fate to that of its parent in a way that confers broader dependency than current practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed rule would link a putative 'child' applications’ fate to that of its 'parent.' The link would be established unidirectionally as an extension of the mechanism that overcomes 'non-statutory double patenting.' Current practice limits term and imposes ownership restrictions to prevent abuse; the proposed linkage goes further and is objectionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO rulemaking must respect the Patent Office's mission and statutory purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO's role is to judge whether the applicant has fairly obtained the exclusive rights granted by the Patent Act, not to abridge those rights or to enact measures outside that purview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any abridgments of these rights or even the simplification of litigation falls outside the purview of the USPTO, no matter how well intentioned. The avowed purpose of the USPTO is detailed under the Patent Act of 1790: it granted the applicant the 'sole and exclusive right and liberty' of making, using, and vending the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed rule should not impose undue cost and complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: A new terminal disclaimer requirement must not create significant additional cost or complexity that disadvantages innovators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtaining a single U.S. patent has an average cost of $20,000 to $30,000; global protection can cost $100,000. The proposed rule will add significant cost and complexity to the current patent process, favoring organizations with large legal budgets and destroying the ability of small and large entities alike to obtain enforceable patents at a reasonable cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality of USPTO-proposed alternatives must be evaluated
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested mechanisms for addressing terminal disclaimer requirements (combine claims, cancel/amend, argue patentable distinctness, file reissue) must be practicable and not impose unrealistic burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The letter addresses each USPTO suggestion: (1) combining conflicting claims into a single application is impractical because there is no practical method to combine claims into an already issued patent; (2) canceling or amending conflicting claims forces applicants to accept flaws or eliminate improved claims (a 'Hobsons choice'); (3) arguing patentable distinctness imposes the burden of substantive office actions; (4) reissue is arduous, expensive, requires surrendering the patent, and may be unavailable due to timing constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confiscation of rights across patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidation of a single claim should not automatically strip rights from other claims or related patents in a continuation chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the current system, invalidation of any one claim does not render the other claims of that patent or any other patent automatically invalid. Under the proposed rules, an applicant seeking a variety of claim coverage through continuation practice will be subject to confiscation of all of its rights if just one claim in an earlier issued patent in the continuation chain is found to be invalid. Such confiscation is untenable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule should not incentivize defensive or inefficient filing strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory changes must not force applicants to adopt filing strategies that increase costs and burden examiners, such as filing parent applications with extremely large claim sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed rule may force innovators to file parent applications with extremely large claim sets, increasing initial drafting costs before knowing the scope of the prior art and increasing the burden on the Examiner. Spreading examination across multiple applications currently provides more focused examination and better claims than forcing examination of a very large number of claims in one examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation must actually achieve stated policy goals
rubrics_metrics.description: A new rule should demonstrably promote competition and simplify patent litigation if those are its stated objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The letter argues both goals will not be achieved: the proposed rule is unlikely to simplify litigation because it is 'so draconian it will never come into effect,' and it will not promote competition because increased costs and limitations will serve entrenched interests rather than innovators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent policy should promote innovation and not favor implementors
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy changes should preserve incentives for innovation by ensuring inventors can profit and compete; undermining effective patents discourages innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If effective patents (with iteratively tuned claims) are prevented by the new rule, then only established non-innovative businesses prosper. Promoting competition means easy access to the patenting of new ideas; crippling costs and confiscation of legitimate claims will favor market power of implementors, not innovators, and will discourage both new innovators and established market leaders from innovating.
